title: Why Oxford–Milton Keynes trains still haven't started: staffing dispute and readiness
label: 4 November 2026 · East West Rail: delivery and delay
summary: Witnesses told the Transport Committee that most physical work to open the Oxford–Milton Keynes section of East West Rail is complete — stations, train modifications and much driver training — but passenger services have been blocked for 744 days mainly by an unresolved union dispute about the role and pay of a second safety‑critical member of staff on trains. The Department, operator Chiltern and the unions are negotiating; officials and managers say the remaining steps are routine (final training, safety validation and approvals) and expect a resolution in weeks rather than years, though no date was set.

speakers.label: Jodie Lofthouse
speakers.name: Jodie Lofthouse
speakers.role: Programme Director for East West Rail, Department for Transport

glossary.definition: Driver-only operation: the driver is the sole safety‑critical staff member responsible for doors and dispatch.
Driver-controlled operation: the driver controls the train but a second staff member can be present with other duties.
Customer Service Inspector: the operator's proposed second on-board person focused on customer service and visibility, not dispatch.
Office of Rail and Road: the rail safety regulator that approves operating methods.
Great British Railways: planned national rail body intended to provide a strategic overview and single employer role.

chapters.title: Why no passenger services yet
chapters.takeaway: Most infrastructure and trains are ready, but services are blocked mainly by an unresolved staffing dispute.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: The line between Oxford and Milton Keynes opened 744 days ago — why has no passenger service yet run?

turns.speaker: Eddie Dempsey
turns.text: There were technical delays and a late contract award after the election, but for us the key issue is staffing: formal consultation on staff arrangements only started in July, and we're still negotiating what the second person on board will do.

turns.speaker: Jodie Lofthouse
turns.text: I share residents' frustration. The Department and Chiltern have completed much of the mobilisation: driver training, train modifications and station work, but we still need an agreed operating model before we set a service date.

turns.speaker: Tony Baxter
turns.text: Chiltern has done the train modifications, recruited and trained drivers, and largely finished station fit-out at Winslow — the remaining blocking point is reaching agreement with the unions on the method of operation.

chapters.title: The unions' safety argument
chapters.takeaway: RMT wants a second safety‑critical staff member with full guard responsibilities; the operator proposes CSIs with limited safety duties — the disagreement is small in pay but central to safety and roles.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: RMT, is this dispute primarily about passenger safety or about jobs and timing?

turns.speaker: Eddie Dempsey
turns.text: It's about passenger safety. We want a second safety‑critical person able to carry out full guard duties: evacuation, protecting the line and managing the platform‑train interface.

turns.speaker: Alex Mayer
turns.text: How many staff are we talking about and what's the pay difference?

turns.speaker: Eddie Dempsey
turns.text: Fewer than 40 people. The difference in pay for a second safety‑critical role is about £5,000 each; the total cost to resolve it is roughly £150k–£200k a year.

turns.speaker: Alex Mayer
turns.text: Is dispatch the main safety concern — why can't the driver handle doors and dispatch?

turns.speaker: Eddie Dempsey
turns.text: Drivers can operate doors, but the platform‑train interface is where many injuries occur; having another trained person to manage dispatch, accessibility and incidents gives extra assurance and can prevent traps and drags.

turns.speaker: Steff Aquarone
turns.text: The ORR considers DOO safe in many cases — why do you disagree with the regulator?

turns.speaker: Eddie Dempsey
turns.text: My experience as a driver and safety rep tells me having staff on board who can carry out full safety duties matters, especially at night and for vulnerable passengers; this is as much about the kind of railway we want as about formal regulation.

turns.speaker: Dave Calfe
turns.text: ASLEF is waiting for the RMT to conclude its talks; we will then discuss driver arrangements. We support a properly crewed railway and aren't rushing into a separate dispute.

chapters.title: Operational readiness and other issues
chapters.takeaway: Train and station work is almost done; outstanding items are union agreement, final training, safety validations and regulatory approvals.

turns.speaker: Tony Baxter
turns.text: We've taken on the 196 trains, completed modifications, recruited 44 drivers and finished most station fit‑outs; Winslow handover is in progress and some legal lease issues are now resolved.

turns.speaker: Alex Mayer
turns.text: How long after an agreement would it take to start services?

turns.speaker: Tony Baxter
turns.text: It's difficult to give a firm date because some final steps need partners' input, but the remaining tasks — updating training, final driver route and train training, and safety validation with the ORR — are routine.

turns.speaker: Jodie Lofthouse
turns.text: The Department supported appointing Chiltern as operator; risks like industrial relations were on our registers and we set escalation routes when they materialised.

turns.speaker: Daniel Francis
turns.text: Does public ownership of Chiltern from September 2026 change the prospects?

turns.speaker: Tony Baxter
turns.text: Not materially. Industrial relations are generally good; being publicly owned doesn't remove the need for approvals and agreements, but we continue to work closely with the Department.

turns.speaker: Dave Calfe
turns.text: One practical lesson: use existing depots. Drivers were initially based at Banbury but work was moved to Bletchley — using the existing depot at Bletchley would have been more efficient.

chapters.title: Lessons learned and next steps
chapters.takeaway: Officials say key lessons are earlier operator involvement and integrated delivery; all parties say they want a quick resolution and expect weeks rather than years, but no firm start date was given.

turns.speaker: Jodie Lofthouse
turns.text: Key lessons for future phases: bring the operator in earlier, adopt a systems view with all delivery partners, and give the delivery body a strong integration role to avoid late changes.

turns.speaker: Tony Baxter
turns.text: Early operating involvement avoids small late changes that cumulatively delay delivery — that includes station fit‑outs and detail design for services.

turns.speaker: Olly Glover
turns.text: What will each of you do next to get the dispute resolved and services running, and when do you think that will happen?

turns.speaker: Dave Calfe
turns.text: ASLEF will engage fully once RMT and Chiltern conclude discussions. I can't give a precise timescale because we're waiting on those talks.

turns.speaker: Tony Baxter
turns.text: Chiltern is focused on negotiations, will keep liaising with the Department and will speed through final ratifications once there is agreement; we don't expect it to be years.

turns.speaker: Jodie Lofthouse
turns.text: The Department will continue to advise Ministers and support Chiltern; it's for Ministers to decide any further action but our objective is to get services running quickly.

turns.speaker: Eddie Dempsey
turns.text: We're in good faith negotiations and hopeful common sense will prevail; we think this could be wrapped up in weeks.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Thank you all. The meeting was illuminating — please follow up in writing if you want to add anything. We'll suspend briefly before the next panel.
